notes.meaning: Joseph told the manager of his house to give the brothers as much grain as they could carry. He also commanded that each brother's payment money be placed back inside his sack. Joseph showed great kindness to his family, while also quietly setting the stage for one final test.

Joseph ordered his personal silver cup to be hidden inside Benjamin's sack along with his grain money. This cup was a large, valuable bowl used for drinking. Joseph set up this situation to see if the older brothers would protect Benjamin or abandon him when trouble came.
At sunrise, the brothers loaded their donkeys and started the journey home. They left Egypt feeling happy and relieved because Simeon was freed and they had eaten a feast with the governor.
Before the brothers traveled far from the city, Joseph sent his house manager to chase after them. The manager was told to stop them and ask why they had repaid Joseph's hospitality with evil.

The manager accused the brothers of stealing the special cup his master used. Ancient rulers claimed to predict the future with such cups. Joseph used this claim as part of his disguise so the brothers would think the Egyptian ruler could uncover secret deeds.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars observe that reading liquids in cups was a widespread Egyptian custom, and Joseph's servant used this well-known practice to emphasize the cup's high value and make the theft seem even worse.

notes.meaning: The manager caught up with the brothers and repeated every word Joseph had commanded. The sudden accusation shocked the men, who believed their troubles in Egypt were finally over.
The brothers immediately declared that they were innocent. They could not believe anyone would accuse them of such a disgraceful crime after how honestly they had tried to act.

To prove their honesty, the brothers reminded the manager that they had returned the money they found in their sacks from their first journey. Since they had willingly brought that silver back from Canaan, they had no reason to steal from the governor's palace.

The brothers were so sure of their innocence that they made a rash promise. They declared that if the cup was found with any of them, that man should be put to death, and all the rest would become slaves.
The manager lessened the harsh punishment they proposed. He declared that only the person caught with the cup would become a slave, while all the other brothers would be completely free to go home.
Without hesitation, each brother quickly brought his sack down to the ground and opened it wide. Because their consciences were clean regarding any theft, they welcomed an immediate search.
The manager searched every sack, starting with Reuben, the oldest, and finishing with Benjamin, the youngest. When he reached the last bag, the silver cup was discovered inside Benjamin's grain.
The brothers tore their clothes in utter grief and horror. Instead of leaving Benjamin behind to save their own lives, every brother loaded his donkey and returned to the city with him.

Judah led the brothers back into Joseph's house, where Joseph was still waiting for them. They threw themselves down to the ground before him in deep sorrow and helplessness, once again fulfilling Joseph's early boyhood dreams.
Joseph confronted them sternly, asking how they could commit such an act. He maintained his Egyptian disguise by asking whether they realized an important man like him could uncover hidden secrets.

Judah admitted that they had no way to defend themselves. He did not mean Benjamin had stolen the cup, but rather that God was finally calling them to account for selling Joseph years earlier. Judah offered that all the brothers would become slaves together.

Joseph rejected Judah's offer and insisted that it would be wrong to punish the innocent. He stated that only Benjamin would remain behind as a slave, while the other brothers were free to return home to their father in peace.
Judah stepped forward to address the ruler directly, begging Joseph not to be angry. He showed deep respect by acknowledging that Joseph held absolute authority, equal to Pharaoh himself.

differ.view: Lutherans often look to Judah's plea as a prime example of heartfelt, bold prayer that clings to mercy before a mighty authority.

notes.meaning: Judah gently reminded Joseph of their very first meeting. He pointed out that the governor had specifically questioned them about their family, asking if they had an aged father or another brother.
Judah repeated their original answer to the ruler. They had explained that their father was old and dearly loved his youngest son, whose only full brother was now dead.
Judah reminded Joseph that he had insisted on seeing the youngest brother in person. The governor had promised that bringing Benjamin would show his goodwill toward them.
Judah explained that they had warned the governor back then about their father's fragile health. If the boy were separated from Jacob, the heartbreak would cause their father to die.
Judah recalled how strict the governor's command had been. Joseph had declared that they would never be permitted to buy food or see his face again unless Benjamin came along.
Judah described returning to Canaan and reporting the ruler's exact demands to their father. Jacob had to face the reality of what the Egyptian governor required.
When their grain ran out, Jacob asked his sons to go back to Egypt to buy a little more food. The ongoing famine left the family with no other way to survive.

The sons reminded Jacob that traveling without Benjamin was useless and dangerous. The Egyptian ruler had clearly warned them that they would not even be admitted into his presence without their youngest brother.
Judah shared Jacob's heartbreaking response with Joseph. Jacob had spoken of Rachel as his true wife, remembering that she had given birth to only two sons.
Judah quoted Jacob's words about the first son who had disappeared years earlier. Jacob had concluded that Joseph was torn to pieces by wild animals, and he had never seen him since that day.
Jacob had pleaded that losing Benjamin on the road would kill him. He warned that such a loss would bring his gray hair down to the grave in unbearable grief.
Judah explained that his father's very life was completely tied to the life of the boy. If Judah returned home without Benjamin, Jacob would not have the strength to carry on.
Judah warned that the moment Jacob saw Benjamin was missing, he would drop dead from sorrow. The brothers could not bear the thought of causing their father's death by leaving the boy behind.

Judah explained his personal duty in the matter. He had promised his father that he would take full responsibility for Benjamin's life and bear the blame forever if he failed to bring him back safely.

Judah made a stunning request: he offered to remain in Egypt as a slave for the rest of his life in Benjamin's place. He pleaded with Joseph to let the boy return safely to Canaan with the other brothers.

differ.view: Reformed teachers see Judah's willing self-sacrifice as a mark of true leadership and a picture of Christ, who substituted Himself to bear the penalty for His people.

notes.meaning: Judah concluded by asking how he could ever face his father without Benjamin by his side. He declared that he would rather live as an Egyptian slave than witness the agony that would destroy his father.
